text: You get an integer n, the number of pairs of parentheses. Return all the strings of well-formed parentheses you can build with them.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — every answer has length two n: exactly n opens and n closes. Well-formed means every close has an open before it to match. And the order of the output doesn't matter. Is that right? So I think the real rule is about prefixes. Read left to right. At every point, the number of closes can never pass the number of opens. And opens can never pass n.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and eight.

OK. At n equals eight there are one thousand four hundred thirty answers. Those counts are the Catalan numbers: one, two, five, fourteen, and so on. The output itself is the big cost, so I just want to build each answer once, with no wasted work. Let me run through the example. n equals three gives five strings, and n equals one gives just one pair. A string like close then open fails, because its first prefix already has more closes than opens.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to list all two to the two n strings of opens and closes, and keep the balanced ones. It works, and I'll use it later as a checker. But almost every string gets thrown away. At n equals eight, that's two to the sixteenth strings to check, just to keep one thousand four hundred thirty. This problem reminds me of the backtracking template: build the answer one character at a time. Here, at each step I have two choices: add an open or add a close. If I only make a choice when it keeps the prefix valid, I never build a bad string. So there's nothing to filter at the end.

Here's the plan. One: track open and close, the counts in the prefix, so I never have to scan the string again. Two: if open is below n, add an open; if close is below open, add a close. Three: when the length reaches two n, save it. One thing worth flagging — the guard close below open is a correctness rule, not a speed-up. Let me walk through that. If I wrote close at most open, then at n equals one I could put a close first. Same for close below n. Both are wrong on all eight sizes. And because the invariant always holds, there are no dead ends. Every call I make reaches at least one answer. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. That matches the plan: the base case saves a full-length string, and two guarded calls add an open or a close. One thing worth flagging — there's no pop here. Res is passed by value, and res plus a character builds a brand-new string, so the caller's res is never changed, and there's nothing to undo. Also, the two branches are two separate ifs on purpose. With else if, I'd only try a close when an open was not allowed, so n equals two gives only one answer. And the base case checks the full length: stopping at open equals n would return a lone open for n equals one.
This works. Can you avoid copying res on every call?

Yes. I'd pass res by reference, push back before each call, and pop back right after it. There's a trade-off here. With a reference, the pop back is required. Without it, the open stays in the string when I try the close branch, and n equals two gives only one answer. The by-value version can't make that mistake. On speed, at n equals eight I measured about zero point three six milliseconds by value and zero point one five by reference. Same big O. The reference is a constant-factor win.

Let's dry-run the code with n equals two, expecting two answers. The row that matters is call six: we are back in call two, and its res is still a single open. Nothing from the first branch leaked in, because each call had its own copy. Now close below open holds, so it adds a close and continues to the second answer. Eight calls, every one led to an answer, no dead ends. That matches. Corner cases: n equals one takes three calls. n equals eight gives one thousand four hundred thirty strings in six thousand nine hundred seventeen calls. Trying the close branch first is still correct, just in reverse order. And against the brute force for n from one to eight, all sizes match with no duplicates.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is O of four to the n over root n. The number of answers is the Catalan number, which grows like four to the n over n to the one point five, and each answer has length two n. Since there are no dead ends, the work is tied to the output. The space complexity is O of n for the recursion depth, not counting the output. With by-value strings, each level holds its own copy, so the live characters add up to O of n squared; the reference version brings that back to O of n. Oh, one more thing — the call counts grow just like the answer counts, ending at six thousand nine hundred seventeen calls for one thousand four hundred thirty answers. That's the no-dead-ends idea in numbers.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed it as a prefix rule, close at most open at most n, and showed it means no dead ends and nothing to filter. You showed close below open and the two separate ifs are needed for correctness, with a counterexample for each. And you explained why there's no pop: by value is safe, and by reference is faster but needs pop back. Good work.
